description: We are students at Boston University's MSBA program.
summary:
We built Rocket Duo, a browser game for one or two players where the team plans and launches a small satellite mission together. The screen is split in two. The Engineer controls the rocket but can’t see what anything means. The Manual Reader has all the mission data but can’t touch the controls. To succeed, they have to talk to each other.

Players go through a full mission: they pick a mission, build a rocket to fit it, choose a launch date by weighing weather against the deadline, run a go/no-go check, and then fix emergencies during flight.

This answers the challenge by turning real mission-design trade-offs into gameplay: payload against fuel, cost against capability, schedule against risk. The rules and numbers come from NASA sources such as CubeSat 101, the CubeSat Design Specification and NASA’s launch weather criteria, and every source is listed in the game.

It matters because space missions are teamwork under pressure. Rocket Duo lets students and the public experience that firsthand.
details:
What it does

Rocket Duo is a cooperative browser game about planning and launching a small satellite mission. It runs on one screen for one or two players. The left side is the Engineer’s console, which shows the rocket and the controls but not what anything means. The right side is the Mission Control Manual, which has all the data but no controls. The team has to share information out loud to make good decisions.

How it works

A full mission has five stages:

Mission. Choose one of three contracts: a CubeSat swarm (Dawn-1), a 3U tech demo (Wingspan), or an ISS supply run (Supply Line). The Engineer reads the mission code, and the Reader looks up the payload, target orbit, budget and deadline.

Assembly. Build the rocket by picking stages, engines and fuel tanks. A heavier payload needs more fuel, and more fuel costs more.

Launch Plan. Pick a launch day using a 7-day weather forecast. Waiting for better weather costs money and time against the deadline.

Launch Prep. Run a go/no-go check and catch fault codes before launch.

Flight. Warnings appear during ascent, such as wind shear, engine overheating or a stage separation fault. The Engineer describes each one, the Reader finds the fix in the manual, and the team has a few seconds to act.

The result screen shows whether the payload reached orbit, and how much budget and time the team used.

Benefits

Players learn real mission trade-offs by making them, instead of reading about them: payload against fuel, cost against capability, schedule against weather risk.

Communication is built into the rules, so the game practices teamwork and clear callouts, the way real launch teams work.

It runs in any browser with no install, and solo players can do both roles.

Expected impact

We designed Rocket Duo for classrooms, outreach events and families. Our goal is to give students and the public a hands-on feel for how space missions are planned, and to show that spaceflight depends on teamwork as much as on technology.

Tools and technology

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript in a single self-contained file, with no frameworks or backend.

HTML Canvas for the animated pixel-art space scene.

Google Fonts (Silkscreen, Chakra Petch) for the retro mission-control style.

GitHub for version control and hosting.

AI tools: Claude helped with coding, UI design and checking sources. Perplexity helped with research. The team checked the facts against the original documents.

What’s innovative

Asymmetric co-op: one player sees, the other knows. This turns mission data into conversation, not just a quiz.

Real data as game rules: values and causes are drawn from NASA sources such as CubeSat 101, the CubeSat Design Specification, NASA launch weather criteria and NASA technical reports. Every claim is listed in an in-game glossary and a SOURCES.md file, with clear labels for what is official NASA data, what is non-official and what is a simplification for gameplay.

What we considered

Scope: we focused on 1–2 players and three missions so the game would be complete and playable within the hackathon.

Accuracy vs. fun: we kept real cause-and-effect but simplified the numbers, and labeled the simplifications.

Accessibility: readable fonts, high-contrast colors, a tutorial, and frames that scroll instead of overflowing.

Honesty: the game says it uses NASA open data but is not an official NASA product.
